title: Colombia’s divided board raises rates as the wage shock reaches expectations
summary: Four Colombian directors voted for a 100 basis point increase to 10.25% at the January meeting, two wanted to cut by 50 basis points and one preferred to hold. The minutes released on 5 February show why the same wage decision produced recommendations 150 basis points apart. The majority believed a sharp rise in expected inflation had already removed the restraint provided by the old nominal interest rate. The two directors favouring a cut placed more weight on supply, indexation and the possibility that high financing costs would reduce production. The hold voter accepted that expectations had risen but questioned how fully wage costs would translate into prices. Those distinctions matter to the rate outlook because the three views predict different responses to the same subsequent inflation or employment release.

The starting point was a year of little progress in headline inflation. December inflation was 5.1%, compared with 5.2% a year earlier. Inflation excluding food and regulated prices rose from 4.85% in November to 5.02% in December, close to its 5.15% reading in December 2024. The majority noted that inflation had ended above target for five consecutive years. What changed fastest was the forward-looking evidence. Between the December and January surveys, the median analyst forecast for end-2026 inflation went from 4.6% to 6.4%; the end-2027 forecast moved from 3.8% to 4.8%. Market-implied inflation also exceeded 6% at the two-year horizon. The increases at longer horizons mattered because an immediate wage adjustment could become more persistent through subsequent price- and wage-setting decisions.

The majority argued that the government’s minimum-wage increase of more than 23% aggravated domestic pressures already apparent in the second half of 2025. A rise of about two percentage points in one-year expected inflation would, at an unchanged nominal rate, lower the forward-looking real rate by roughly the same amount. In the majority’s judgment that left policy around neutral when conditions called for restraint. A one-point nominal hike restored only part of the lost restraint. These four directors accordingly described this decision as the beginning of a fresh tightening cycle. They saw early action as a way to restore credibility and reduce the eventual output and employment costs of adjustment. The minutes’ closing position for the Board as a whole kept future decisions conditional on incoming information.

The evidence on demand helps explain why the majority saw substantial scope for cost increases to pass through. Staff estimated 2025 growth at 2.9%. Private and public consumption were strong, while preliminary capital-goods imports pointed to a more modest recovery in machinery and equipment investment. Staff estimated that the output gap had been positive since at least the third quarter of 2024 and had widened near the end of 2025. The estimated current account deficit increased from 1.6% of GDP in 2024 to 2.4% in 2025. Imports rose strongly alongside domestic demand. Manufacturing, agriculture and service exports improved, but lower mining and energy exports held down aggregate export growth. A wage increase could also raise public expenditure through pensions and other items, adding a fiscal channel to the direct effect on labour costs.

The dissenting directors provided competing mechanisms that can be tested. Those favouring a cut pointed to regulated and food prices, supply shocks and indexation. They expected oil prices and peso appreciation to allow the government to lower fuel prices, and warned that more expensive credit could reduce supply and add to prices. They also highlighted the distributional gains from higher labour income and the risks to a recovery led by domestic consumption. The hold voter stressed the potential for firm margins to absorb part of the increase. Research on markups and pay relative to marginal productivity, cited by this director, concerns particular sectors. It establishes a possible channel without measuring economy-wide pass-through of this wage adjustment. A divergence between prices in labour-intensive services and sectors with greater scope to compress margins would bear directly on the disagreement.

The Spanish capital-markets annex puts dates and instruments around the repricing. Its Tables 1–2 report one-year inflation compensation averaging 6.35% in the January sample through the 23rd, up 138 basis points from the December average. The 23 January point estimate was 6.96%, up 213 basis points from 19 December. The bank survey’s end-2026 forecast rose from 4.59% to 6.37%, while its fixed one-year measure rose from 4.59% to 6.15%. These are distinct ways to observe the change that the majority summarised as roughly two points. Bond inflation compensation also reflects pricing and liquidity. The annex describes thin trading amid concerns over inflation, fiscal risks and government financing. Its charts 51–52 show the 12-month IBR benchmark and 12-month overnight-indexed swap rate rose 94 and 97 basis points from 19 December to 23 January. Much of that repricing occurred between 29 December and 2 January, when those rates rose 70 and 66 basis points respectively. Both windows end before the Board decision. They measure investors’ adjustment around the wage news and other intervening developments; a separate announcement-window observation is needed to identify the market response to the actual 100 basis point vote.

questions.question: How widely did the wage shock pass through into prices rather than margins?
questions.detail: The competing votes hinge on whether firms could absorb the wage increase and whether domestic demand allowed them to pass it on. Compare post-adjustment prices and volumes across industries with different minimum-wage exposure, allowing for regular repricing dates, regulated prices and food supply. Pair official inflation components with wage, employment and corporate-margin evidence. Broad price acceleration alongside resilient volumes would give a different reading from margin compression concentrated in exposed sectors.

questions.question: How much of the 100 basis point increase had markets already anticipated?
questions.detail: The annex reports a large pre-meeting adjustment in IBR and OIS, yet the one-year instruments cover multiple future meetings. Recover expected near-term rates from contracts bracketing the decision and examine the shortest available announcement window, documenting liquidity and simultaneous fiscal or external news. Compare subsequent maturities to separate surprise about this meeting from repricing of the tightening cycle. The December-to-January changes alone cannot answer either question.

questions.question: Does higher financing cost damp demand faster than it limits productive supply?
questions.detail: The majority’s positive output gap and the dissenters’ supply concern make different predictions for business credit, equipment orders, employment and pricing. Track official bank-lending conditions and investment alongside consumer spending, imports and unemployment. Contrast highly credit-dependent sectors with others and distinguish borrowing costs from credit demand. The timing matters because the initial cost shock and the later effect on spending can both occur within the same tightening episode.

limitation: The English minutes cover the full Board discussion. The separate Spanish capital-markets and statistical annexes supply supporting material. The figures discussed here use selected tables and charts in the capital-markets annex.
